title: Teaching
text:
Child Development and Social Policy in a Global Society (APSY-UE 1279) | Spring 2026
Undergraduate, Department of Applied Psychology, New York University
Course description: How does social policy shape children’s lives? And how do children’s needs shape social policy? This course explores these questions through interdisciplinary, philosophical, theoretical, and historical lenses, at national and global scales. Students gain tools to understand the role contextual forces play in children’s development and how social policy can, in turn, foster that development. We also examine the policymaking process itself, including the roles that advocates, philanthropists, researchers, and policymakers play in addressing key issues, through readings, activities, and conversations with experts. By the end of the course, students are able to critically engage with the diverse perspectives underlying policymaking, discuss child development within complex policy contexts, and evaluate whether and how social policies respond to children’s needs.

Teaching Assistant, Policy Graduate Program, Wagner School of Public Policy, New York University

Students apply each method in Stata and estimate their own model in a final project.

title: Strengthening Programs and Their Implementation
text:
Illustration by Storyset
In partnership with education agencies, I study how education systems and the services they deliver can be strengthened. This work asks both whether programs foster children’s development and how they are put into practice: what supports successful implementation, and how effective programs can be improved and scaled equitably. With New York City Public Schools, this includes evaluations of the city’s universal pre-K professional learning and arts integration programs, and an ongoing study of a strings-based arts program in pre-K through grade 2. I have also partnered with education agencies in Argentina, Peru, and Latvia.

title: Access to Education
text:
Illustration by Storyset
Before children can benefit from high-quality programs, they have to get into them. In partnership with education agencies, I study the challenges families face in gaining access to schools and programs, and I develop and evaluate tools and system-level changes to address them. My Choice-in-Context model frames family decision-making within the structures of choice systems, showing how family, system, and context factors interact to produce inequities, rather than treating disparities as the result of family preferences alone. This model guides my dissertation, conducted with the New York City Public Schools Student Enrollment Office, which includes an early warning system that uses machine learning to identify families at risk of not enrolling in preschool. This is the focus of my future research agenda.

title: Berta Bartoli
text:
Berta Bartoli
PhD Candidate, New York University
 Email  CV  GitHub


I am a PhD candidate in Psychology and Social Intervention at New York University, where my research bridges psychology, education policy, and quantitative methods to understand how social and institutional contexts shape children’s access to educational opportunities. Through interdisciplinary research and partnerships with policymakers and practitioners, I seek to generate evidence and develop practical tools that make early education systems more equitable, accessible, and responsive to the needs of children and families.
My research interests are primarily motivated by my experiences growing up in Caracas, Venezuela, where I witnessed stark inequities in children’s access to educational opportunities. I am committed to contributing to our understanding of educational access and how it can be strengthened in ways that enable policy leaders to build systems for all.
My research has been funded by the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) and the National Science Foundation (NSF), as an IES Predoctoral Interdisciplinary Research Training (PIRT) fellow and a recipient of the American Educational Research Association (AERA)–NSF Dissertation Grant. I was also named a semifinalist for the National Academy of Education/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship.



I hold an M.S.Ed. in Statistics, Measurement, Assessment, Research and Technology from the University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education, and a B.A. in Economics and International Affairs, magna cum laude (minors in Mathematics, Psychology, and Business Administration), from Northeastern University.

title: Early Childhood Strings Program
text:
Illustration by Storyset

The Early Childhood Strings Program brings violin instruction into New York City Public Schools classrooms from pre-K through grade 2, with the aim of narrowing early learning gaps, particularly in literacy. Through an ongoing partnership with the NYCPS Arts Office, our team supports the implementation and evaluation of the program. In 2026, we conducted an implementation study to understand how the program is put into practice and the mechanisms through which learning the violin may shape children’s learning and development. In 2027, we will conduct an impact study of the program.
Team: NYU Institute of Human Development and Social Change (PI: Pamela Morris-Perez)
Role: Graduate Assistant, April 2025–present

title: Determinants of Educational Opportunity
text:
Illustration by Storyset
Children develop within distinct but interconnected contexts: their families, their schools, and the broader social and structural systems around them. Drawing on ecological systems theory and interdisciplinary perspectives, I study how these contexts shape children’s learning, development, and access to educational opportunity, and how these processes vary across children and communities. This work grounds my partnership research: understanding the contexts children grow up in helps identify where systems can best support them.

title: Research
text:
My research is motivated by a central question: how can we empower caregivers and create systems that make high-quality educational opportunities more equitable and accessible?
I study the full trajectory of educational opportunity: how children’s homes, schools, and broader structural contexts shape their access to opportunity; how education systems can deliver high-quality programs, with attention not only to whether they work but to how they are implemented; and how families gain access to those systems in the first place. My work is interdisciplinary, uses quantitative and qualitative methods, and is conducted in partnership with education agencies in New York City and around the world. I am currently most interested in access to high-quality early childhood education.

Research Areas










Determinants of Educational Opportunity


How children’s homes, schools, and broader structural contexts shape their learning, development, and access to opportunity.












Strengthening Programs and Their Implementation


Whether education programs work, and the conditions under which they can be implemented well, improved, and scaled.












Access to Education


How families navigate choice and enrollment in education systems, and what systems can do to support them. My work has focused on access to early education programs.
